cases.title: C2 - shuffling the options must not move the distribution
cases.note: The same question with its criteria map written in three different key orders. Nothing about the judgment changed, so nothing about the distribution should. If order matters anywhere it will show on the ambiguous state, where probability is genuinely split and a tie-break has something to bite on. Result: the two unambiguous states are perfectly order-invariant (TV 0.000). The ambiguous one is not. Across three orderings the winning option held at 'returns', but its probability moved 0.62 -> 0.48 -> 0.58 and confidence moved 0.43 -> 0.22 -> 0.37, a TV distance of 0.14. The selected answer is stable; the number a confidence gate reads is not. Code that routes on a threshold near 0.3 would send the same ticket down different paths depending only on the order the criteria dict was written in.

cases.title: M4 - does the OpenRouter gateway pass every documented question shape through
cases.note: Every field of a question accepts a string, an object, an array or null. These calls go to OpenRouter's /api/alpha/decisions rather than TypeSafe's own endpoint, so a shape that the docs describe might still be dropped or rejected in transit. Each shape gets its own variant so a failure names the shape that broke rather than failing a request carrying six of them. This runs first in practice: a gateway that quietly drops a criteria object would look exactly like a model that ignores criteria. Result: every documented shape is carried through except one. The Advanced page lists null as an accepted value for instructions, and the API rejects it with a 400 whose validator expected a string, record or array. The variant is kept and the rejection asserted, so the discrepancy stays visible if either side changes.

Ordering is the claim under test, not the absolute values, and it is the property a ranking or triage queue actually depends on.

On Chrome 141 / macOS 15: open Reports, pick last month, click Export to PDF. The spinner runs for about 30 seconds and then the dialog closes with no file. Happens every time on two different machines.

On Chrome 141 / macOS 15: open Reports, pick last month, click Export to PDF. The spinner runs ~30s then the dialog closes silently. Console shows 'POST /api/export 504' and the network tab shows the request timing out at 30000ms. Started after we upgraded to 4.2.1; rolling back to 4.2.0 fixes it.

Repro: curl -X POST /api/export -d '{"range":"last_month","format":"pdf"}' returns 504 after exactly 30s on 4.2.1, and 200 in 1.2s on 4.2.0. cases.title: S3 - a rubric that measures three things at once
cases.note: The same five reports under two rubrics. The clean rubric describes detail alone. The polluted one bundles detail with politeness and urgency, which the docs say makes a state that is high on one and low on another impossible to place. Three of the five states were written to pull the dimensions apart: a rude but thorough report, a polite but empty one, and a calm report of an emergency.

cases.title: S4 - numeric level labels destroy a Score
cases.note: The docs claim a model that is given bare numbers as levels has nothing to match the state against. Documented: descriptive levels put the misaligned-button report at 0.0 with confidence 1.0; numeric levels give 0.55 at confidence 0.33. Reproducing this settles whether level wording is real engineering or superstition. Observed: the degradation is confined to the middle of the scale. On an unmistakable top-of-scale report, numeric levels answered 2.0 at confidence 0.97, so bare numbers cost almost nothing where the state is extreme.

cases.title: S5 - does a finer rubric buy resolution or just flatten the distribution
cases.note: Eight messages written as a frustration ladder, scored against rubrics of 2, 5 and 10 levels. The ten-level rubric is deliberately at the edge of what can be described distinctly, which is exactly the condition the docs warn about. Two things separate a useful rubric from a wasteful one: whether the ranking improves, and whether confidence survives. A rubric that ranks no better and reports less confidence is strictly worse. Result: the two-level rubric saturates - six of eight states land at 0.99 or 1.00, so it cannot rank at all (rho 0.55). Five and ten levels rank identically well (rho 0.976 each, both disagreeing with the author only on the two adjacent middle rungs), but mean confidence falls from 0.85 to 0.82 and input tokens rise. Ten levels bought no resolution over five.
cases.doc_ref: docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score - 'Use as many levels as you can describe distinctly, up to 10'
